confidence_note: Thiel's favorite interview question, 'What important truth do very few people agree with you on?', opens Zero to One, and his chapter on secrets argues that great companies are built on secrets: important truths that are not yet widely recognized. He describes three kinds of things: easy (conventions), hard (secrets) and impossible (mysteries), and argues that people stopped looking for secrets because of incrementalism, risk aversion, complacency and 'flatness'. He cites Airbnb and Uber/Lyft as companies built on secrets hidden in plain sight: underused resources people didn't think to use. facts: Thiel's favorite interview question is: 'What important truth do very few people agree with you on?'
He says it is hard to answer: it takes knowledge to find such a truth and courage to say it out loud.
He argues that every great business is built around a secret: an important truth that others haven't recognized yet.
He distinguishes conventions (easy truths everyone knows), secrets (hard but achievable truths) and mysteries (impossible to know).
He argues many people stopped believing in secrets, because of incrementalism, risk aversion, complacency and the belief that everything worth knowing is already known.
He points to companies like Airbnb and Uber as examples: they saw value in underused resources, spare rooms and idle cars, that were in plain sight.
His advice: look for secrets in places no one else is looking.
tension: If a big opportunity were obvious, someone would already have taken it. So where do new ones come from?
opening_idea: An investor asks every candidate one question most people can't answer well.

lessons.idea: Big opportunities hide in unpopular truths.
